candidate.blueprint_topic: Safety and Infection Prevention and Control — body-fluid/regulated medical waste handling
candidate.educational_objective: Manage suctioned body-fluid waste according to the facility's regulated-medical-waste plan and applicable state/local requirements, recognizing that sanitary-sewer disposal is acceptable only where permitted.

options.A: Follow the facility regulated-medical-waste plan and applicable state/local requirements; sanitary-sewer disposal may be used when those requirements permit it
options.B: Always place the entire filled canister in regular trash because suctioned fluids are not regulated medical waste
options.C: Always pour suctioned fluids into any available sink regardless of local sewer-discharge rules
options.D: Always place every suction canister in a sharps container even when no sharps are present

candidate.rationale: CDC guidance states that bulk blood and bloody body-fluid specimens are major categories requiring special handling and that federal, state, and local requirements determine regulated-medical-waste practices. CDC also states that sanitary sewers may be used for blood and suctioned fluids when local sewage-discharge requirements are met and the state accepts that disposal method. Therefore the nurse should follow the facility's approved waste plan and applicable jurisdictional rules rather than assume one disposal route is universal. A is the best answer.
candidate.source_claim_supported: Suctioned body fluids do not have one universal disposal route; disposal must follow the approved waste plan and applicable jurisdictional requirements, with sanitary-sewer disposal permitted in jurisdictions that allow it.
